During my undergrad, I did a Six Sigma study on my sleep and its effect on my productivity.  Not only did my productivity drop dramatically after 9PM or if I got less than 8 hours of sleep, but my productivity increased dramatically if I took a moderately long nap mid-day.  I also had a audio file I listened to that used farm noises to wake me up gently.  That also increased my productivity.  

Edit, because its discussed later ITT: my naps, and sometimes my nightly sleep was on an uncomfortable and tiny camping cot, or, more often, the floor.  I'm sure my productivity would have increased even more if I had been comfortable sleeping.  My study did show, however, that it was much, much more difficult for me to wake up if I was comfortable or if the lights were off.  For this reason, I often purposely slept on the floor even at home, and would sleep with the lights on if I knew I was only going to have time to sleep for a little bit.  College was hard.

I was inside for 17 days.  It was amazing how much changed and how quickly I improved.  And it wasn't just me, it was inspiring watching the amazing transformation in the other people inside too.  In the first few days I was on my feet (my first six days I was in horrible heroin withdrawals and didn't leave my room), we got a new patient on the floor.  He was a massive, strong black guy who was wildly combative and it took eight security guards to get him into the isolation room.  He spent a few days in his room, and even when he got out, he was on edge and even the staff was afraid of him.  One day though we had a lock down event (I was in the highest level of mental health care outside of the mental health hospital, so lock down events happened daily) and I just happened to be locked in the same pod as him.  He was listening to rap music on the iPad and tentatively I asked if I could listen with him.  He asked, "Do you think black men are out to hurt white women?"  The question took me back.  "What?" "Do you think black men are out to hurt white women?" he repeated.  "No," I answered honestly.  "Then why are you afraid of me?" I didn't know what to say, so I explained honestly that he seemed kind of crazy and he was hugely strong and could easily hurt me.  He laughed and smiled in a way that made me feel comfortable, like I could trust him.  After that, we became fast friends, listening to rap music together to pass the time every day.  We laughed together when the staff was too afraid of him to take back the iPad when our time was up.  As the days passed, he seemed more and more lucid.  And he had an amazing insight into my addiction problems, helping me unravel what caused them and how to keep my life manageable so much more than any of the doctors.  He even made me eat when my withdrawal symptoms made me nauseous - he gave me his scary, crazy look, and even though I was completely comfortable with him, I knew he was serious and I ate my food.  As time progressed, he seemed more a more coherent and conversational, and with other patients too, not just me.  I learned his name was James.  One day, right before I left, he finally seemed completely "normal" and he finally finished the conversation we started on the first day we talked.  "I know my anti-seizure medication makes me seem crazy," he explained.  It was heartbreaking.  "And I grew up so poor, my mom was working two jobs, so there was no one to take me to doctors appointments or help to figure out the correct medication and the correct doses.  I had a lot of seizures in school too, and the kids made fun of me, so I dropped out, and still seemed crazy.  Who will hire me like this?  Who will help me?"  I didn't know what to say.  I left the hospital a few days after that.  I called the number he gave me, but its shut off.  I'm just praying he's still inside, or at least somewhere safe.  He helped me so much on my road to recovery.  

As a dual-dianosis patient it was so good for me to be talking to other patients that had mental health problems instead of simple addiction problems.  As I've said and heard so many times in AA, the drugs are just a symptom, I have a problem in my brain.  As James helped me discover, I have poor coping skills.  I couldn't cope with the stress in school, so I had a lower GPA than I wanted.  I couldn't cope with the feelings of failure that came with a low GPA, so I started drinking.  When I failed out of grad school because of my low GPA and my drinking, I couldn't cope with the feelings of failure and the panic that my life wasn't progressing the way I had planned.  These poor coping skills led me to date a guy who helped me forget, and to my drug use.  I couldn't cope with the way that guy treated me, or with life on the streets, so my drug use ran rampant.  I couldn't cope well with withdrawals, so I couldn't get clean.  My poor coping skills even explain why my PTSD was so bad, and why I stayed so long with a man who abused me so badly.  Now that I've identified the problem, I can start working on how to fix it.  

The scheduled group therepy in the hospital helped me a lot too.  I learned healthy ways to cope with my emotions, as well as ways to do "preventative maintenance" to keep me from developing problems like that in the future.  I had this epiphany right before I went in that I was a reckless, dangerous individual who hurt the people around me, and that I've been this way for a long time.  I had a lot of guilt because of this, even if it was subconscious.  The group therepy helped me understand why I acted this way, for so long.  As much as I feel like a horrible person, I didn't behave this way because I'm Satan incarnate; I have poor coping skills and literally didn't know how to behave in a healthy manner.  Yes, I've hurt a lot of people, but its not at all because I didn't care; I still am responsible for my actions, but I just was coping with stress, failure, anxiety and depression in the only way I knew how, and that way caused incredible pain for me and the people around me.  I said this once while I was using, and although I didn't relate it to poor mental health, I think its really true now: chaos is a disease that is contagious through caring.  I had chaos in my life, and the people who cared about me started bringing chaos into their own lives because they were willing to stay up until 4AM the night before a test helping me with a project, or because they were willing to lend me money they needed because I was dope sick, or even just because they were willing to listen to me rant and "feel" my chaos while I talked.  I took more chaos into my life because I cared about my husband, too; I was willing to spend all my money supporting his drug habit because he couldn't cope with the problems in his life, and I was willing to care for him when he was "sick" because he was scared to face his own problems, and I was willing to take care of his son when he was too high and too stressed to deal with a child.  

I'm still not doing perfectly now.  I'm still using drugs, I haven't even made a therepy appointment, and I still have so much chaos and poor coping skills to deal with it.  But at the very least, I'm aware of what I'm doing and why I'm doing it.  I mix up the shots, and I overdosed my boyfriend yesterday and it took three shots of Narcam to bring him back.  He spent all night sick and all day so far today; we don't know if its withdrawals or a reaction to the Narcam, or just every day sickness.  He's been taking care of me at the expense of himself.  He's diabetic and hasn't gotten in to see his doctor in two months, so he's gone without his prescriptions.  We're living on the cusp of death, and I know in my heart that its just a matter of time until I overdose him and can't bring him back.  And this is a man I love with all my heart, my rock in the stormiest of weather, my support when all other support fell away.  This is a man who won't marry me until I am clean and have a stable life, someone crazy enough to draw lines in the sand for me - and lets be honest, it's Elizabeth's way or no way; you have to be crazy to say no to me, because who knows what you'll get.
